internalProposal.label: Dutch language foundations with comparative literature, art and film

course.name: Personal & Professional Development
course.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
course.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
course.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
course.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courseEvidence.contribution: Academic reading, writing, source appraisal and civic reflection.

course.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
course.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
course.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
course.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
course.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

courseEvidence.contribution: Neural signalling, cognition and behaviour prepare experimental language study.

course.name: Introduction to Western Art History
course.description2: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences.
course.profile: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
course.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
course.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis

courseEvidence.contribution: Western painting analysis and a visual-analysis paper provide an art-historical foundation.

course.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
course.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
course.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
course.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
course.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

courseEvidence.contribution: Close reading and interpretation of fiction, drama and poetry.

course.name: Dutch
course.description2: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
course.profile: Develops beginner Dutch for everyday oral and written communication while introducing Dutch culture. Speaking and listening receive particular emphasis, supported by pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, reading and functional writing. Students practise introductions, family conversations, shopping, travel and leisure through dialogues, role-play and short written tasks. Cultural work includes research and presentations in English, engagement with Dutch film and music, and comparison with students’ own cultural contexts.
course.topics: Dutch pronunciation and spelling; Everyday vocabulary for introductions, family, shopping, travel and leisure; Verb conjugation and the perfect tense; Pronouns and possession; Negation; Main- and subordinate-clause word order; Adjectives, comparatives and superlatives; Functional reading and writing; Everyday Dutch cultural practices; Cross-cultural comparison
course.methods: Dutch pronunciation practice; Dialogue construction and conversational role-play; Functional writing in Dutch; Comparative cultural analysis

courseEvidence.contribution: Beginner Dutch listening, speaking, reading and functional writing, with Dutch film, music and culture.

course.name: Psycholinguistics
course.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

courseEvidence.contribution: Bilingualism, language acquisition and experimental language methods within a broader cognitive course.

course.name: Style & Meaning
course.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
course.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
course.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
course.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

courseEvidence.contribution: Stylistic analysis of linguistic choices and literary meaning.

course.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
course.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
course.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
course.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
course.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

courseEvidence.contribution: Interview, ethnographic, documentary and qualitative interpretation methods.

course.name: Modern History
course.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
course.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
course.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
course.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

courseEvidence.contribution: Modern economic and political history situates Dutch questions in wider historical change.

course.name: History of Empires
course.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
course.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
course.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
course.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development

courseEvidence.contribution: Comparative empire, imperial legacies and historical research methods.

course.name: Introduction to Film & Media
course.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
course.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
course.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence
course.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research

courseEvidence.contribution: Film form, cinematography, editing and historical interpretation.

course.name: World Myth & Literature
course.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
course.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
course.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
course.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation

courseEvidence.contribution: Comparative myth and literature, with transmission and cultural interpretation.

course.name: Great Literary Works
course.description2: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
course.profile: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
course.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
course.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

courseEvidence.contribution: Literary texts, genres and critical comparison across periods.

course.name: Life & Travel Writing
course.description2: Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.
course.profile: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.
course.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity
course.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing

courseEvidence.contribution: Memoir, autobiography and travel writing give narrative and intercultural methods.

course.name: The Documentary
course.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
course.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
course.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
course.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

courseEvidence.contribution: Nonfiction audiovisual interpretation and documentary practice.

course.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
course.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.
course.profile: Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice. Students move from lyric foundations to constrained and experimental forms, attending to sound, rhythm, imagery, voice and embodiment. Close reading and creative workshops lead into an independent traditional or hybrid project grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require students to justify formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
course.topics: Meaning and formal experimentation; Lyric poetry; Poetic sound and rhythm; Imagery and voice; Embodiment and performance; Constraint and formal deviation; Experimental poetry; Hybrid and digitally mediated forms; Creative process and revision; Aesthetic traditions and conceptual coherence
course.methods: Close poetic reading and listening; Constraint-based composition; Poetic and performative experimentation; Structured drafting and revision; Critical analysis of creative decisions; Independent practice-based creative inquiry

courseEvidence.contribution: Creative writing, poetry and critical communication practice.

course.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
course.description2: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
course.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
course.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
course.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research

courseEvidence.contribution: Advanced art inquiry and museum analysis within broad modern art.

course.name: European Union Politics
course.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
course.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
course.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
course.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis

courseEvidence.contribution: EU institutions, empirical legislative research and comparative governance context.

course.name: Film & Text
course.description2: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
course.profile: Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory. Students compare plot, structure, characterization and setting with cinematic image, acting, editing, music and sound. Medium specificity, fidelity, intertextuality, auteurism, heritage and adaptation markets frame theoretical debates. A substantial research project applies selected concepts to literary and film material, developing an independent interpretation and leading a text- and film-based discussion.
course.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion
course.methods: Formalist literary analysis; Close film-sequence analysis; Comparative text-film analysis; Intertextual analysis; Theory-led adaptation research

courseEvidence.contribution: Adaptation and close film/literature analysis.

course.name: Persuasive Communication
course.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
course.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
course.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
course.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

courseEvidence.contribution: Persuasion theory, framing and public communication analysis.

course.name: Writing Art's Histories
course.description2: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

courseEvidence.contribution: History and methods of art history through critical readings and disciplinary debates.

course.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
course.description2: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

courseEvidence.contribution: Interpretive theory and a research project on literary meaning.

course.name: Researching the “American Century”
course.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

courseEvidence.contribution: Sustained historical inquiry and source criticism with a specifically American focus.

course.name: Rhetoric in Action
course.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
course.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
course.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
course.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation

courseEvidence.contribution: Rhetorical practice with local schoolchildren, mainly in Dutch. This is community engagement without advanced Dutch-language instruction.

candidateFindings: The strongest feasible challenge combines beginning Dutch and Dutch cultural materials with language acquisition, stylistics, painting, literary interpretation and film. Art, museum and historical methods have real relevance, with broader geographical coverage. The advanced work is mainly comparative or outside Dutch studies. Rhetorical practice in Dutch is engagement rather than language progression. A linguistics-focused variant would require advanced Dutch structure, historical development or multilingual policy across several courses. A culture-focused variant would need sustained Netherlands-centred literature, history, art and film beyond a small set of cultural topics. The proposal is evidence for reassessment after the full target ledger is established.
